comments.author: @YesImaDesigner
comments.text:
Thanks to everyone who shared their thoughts here, whether positive or critical. I know "AI art" is a sensitive and divisive topic, and I completely respect the concerns many of you have raised.

To be clear: I don’t see AI as a replacement for creativity or design. I still start every project with sketches, ideas, and decisions that come from me. Tools like Adobe Firefly are just one part of my process, helping me iterate faster and explore different directions. As stated in the video I don’t ever use generated images as final output, I use them for inspiration, reference, or pieces I can adapt.

I’ve been working as a designer for over 20 years, and my goal with this channel has always been to share how new tools – whether Photoshop, Illustrator, or now AI – can fit into a designer’s workflow without replacing design fundamentals. You don’t have to agree with my take, but I hope we can keep this space open for discussion and learning.

I truly value all of you in this community, even if we see things differently. Thanks for watching and for holding me accountable as I continue to explore where design and technology meet.

I understand the concerns many of you have raised regarding the use of AI, and I want to offer a different perspective on Martin's approach. There appears to be a significant misunderstanding of his intent.

He is not using AI to generate final work to claim as his own. Rather, he is conducting a rigorous exploration of its potential as a tool within his existing workflow—a process that begins and ends with his own original sketches. This is an investigation into its utility for ideation and iteration, maintaining full artistic control and transparency.

For those unfamiliar with Martin's work, his expertise as a masterful designer and illustrator is well-established and unquestionable. A review of his portfolio would immediately confirm his exceptional skill and reputation. His exploration of AI should be viewed as an experienced artist assessing a new technology to add to his arsenal, not as a replacement for the core abilities he has spent a career cultivating.

While the strong reaction from the artistic community comes from a valid place of concern for the craft, in this instance, it is misdirected. Martin's methodology is both ethical and innovative, representing a forward-thinking approach to evolving an artistic process without compromising integrity.

comments.author: @scw55
comments.text:
It depends if you consider yourself artist and/or if you consider yourself as a designer.

If you regard yourself as an artist, I still strongly think generative AI does not produce art. Using a base sketch helps, but the rendering afterwards is not art.

As a designer, where it’s more umbrella, and the priority is the result, not the journey, you still have an issue where the generated image will have errors in it. If you had made the whole thing by hand, those mistakes would simply be your human fingerprint. If it’s machine-generated mistakes, it now becomes “insufficient quality control if you don’t fix them post-generation.”

Interestingly, the user needs to pay to generate the image. It’s money going to Adobe and not another artist whose style options you’d think would work well, and would use that money as income.

One risk with using generated images as moodboard/references/inspiration is that it has been shown that generative AI compounds biases. As you say, you need to ensure you’re in control of the creative process. Which I would ask, wouldn’t you have to be less alert if you didn’t use generative AI? The only motivation I can see for using it in workflow is: curiosity or a tight deadline. Creative deadlines are often pressured by our Capitalist society, who care about efficiency and economic value only.

In a vacuum, the video is quite interesting, and the tool looks fun to experiment with. But we’re not in a vacuum. And there’s still a lot of work that needs to be done in legal systems to ensure no one is getting exploited by this Pandora’s Box.

FOR THOSE WHO ARE GETTING "Input must be a List[Union[str, AddedToken]]" error TRY THIS TO FIX IT. IT WORKED FOR ME

First go to "C:\Users\Usuario\AppData\Local\Programs\ComfyUI\resources\ComfyUI\requirements.txt" and there change the tokenizer and transformers to this version:

transformers>=4.38.2,<4.39.0
tokenizers>=0.15.2,<0.16.0

Save the .txt file and relaunch ComfyUI. ComfyUI should downgrade the version of the tranformers and tokenizers to the working ones.

If it works for you then im happy. U may run to other errors, so I will give the fixes that I found.


If u are missing some dependencies (of the Florence2Model) run this command on the ComfyUI terminal:

& "E:\YOUR_COMFYUI\.venv\Scripts\python.exe" -m pip install matplotlib timm pillow peft accelerate
